source.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table text is flattened, but the reported results and relevant table layouts are generally identifiable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes and decoding conditions affect harmful-prompt refusal, using attack success rates on compressed and base models. This is a conceptual test of V4 in a compression setting, not a test of the specified fine-tuning or token-position KL claims.
record.gate_note: Table 4 reports harmful-prompt attack success rates for vanilla, decoding, and suffix conditions; rows below cover the two decoding measures and suffix measure. Figures 3–6 report directional ablation and activation-addition outcomes, but these test a residual-stream direction, not safety localization in a small set of weights or ranks; those rows are recorded as none. The AIRD results are omitted because they evaluate the paper’s proposed mitigation, not the claim versions. The paper does not measure per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, fine-tuning, or the cause of shallow safety.
record.test_reason: The study measures how pruning and quantization change the refusal direction and harmful-prompt ASR. Decoding and GCG-suffix attacks (borrowed from Wei et al. 2024) are only probes of compressed-model safety. The paper never asks whether these attacks defeat refusal in aligned models, and Table 4's column identities are too garbled to read the attack-vs-vanilla comparison. It also does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefilling, weight localisation, causes of shallowness, or deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Fuller version: refusal stays mediated by one direction after compression. Pruning shifts that direction's source position and orientation (low cosine similarity), quantization preserves it, and the authors offer this as why quantized models are safer. AIRD cuts pruned-model ASR by up to 41% with no significant zero-shot benchmark change and leaves the refusal direction intact.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines compression, refusal-direction interventions, and adversarial safety evaluations rather than fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or measuring token-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies across model, compression method, and attack condition. Table 4 reports two decoding measures; the paper also describes decoding results with and without an [INST] wrapper.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning (Wanda, Magnitude) shifts the refusal direction's layer and token position and lowers its cosine similarity to the original (0.34–0.90). Quantization keeps it (≥0.99). The authors correlate the shift with higher ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning, but not 8-bit quantization, alters the refusal direction and reduces safety of aligned Llama models.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the refusal direction in compressed models raises harmful-prompt attack score; adding it induces refusal on harmless prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal remains mediated by a single residual-stream direction after compression.

record.problems: The paper uses substring matching to classify refusal. Several intervention outcomes are only shown in figures, without extractable numerical values in the text. Table 4’s extracted layout interleaves the Llama2 Wanda rows, so those assignments rely on the visible table structure. The study covers only the stated Llama model families and compression settings.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 4 vanilla ASR rows because they are reference conditions rather than decoding or suffix interventions; their values are included as baselines where used. Omitted AIRD outcome tables and performance benchmarks because they evaluate the paper’s proposed mitigation rather than a claim version.

untested.parts: No per-token KL across response positions.
Prefilling not tested. Decoding and suffix attacks are used only as evaluation probes, and the uncompressed attack-vs-vanilla comparison is not interpretable from the extracted table.
Refusal is studied as a residual-stream direction; weight or rank localisation is not tested.
Causes of shallowness are not examined.
No deepening training; AIRD is a weight edit for compressed models, not token-depth alignment.

missing.what: Cosine similarity of compressed vs original refusal directions (e.g., Llama2 Magnitude 0.337, LLM.int8() 0.996).
Shift in the refusal direction's layer/position under pruning but not quantization.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels are dropped: the attacks are tools for evaluating compression, not tests of V4. Table 4 is internally implausible as read (suffix and decoding ASR below vanilla for Llama2). This suggests the first column may actually be vanilla, which would flip several states. Refusal is classified by substring matching only. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Compliant-opening prefills are not tested. The paper tests adversarial suffixes and decoding conditions, not all bypass methods named in the version.
The study finds a residual-stream refusal direction but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
The data or training objective as a cause of safety shallowness.
Training to spread safety across response tokens and whether such training holds up.

relation.reason: Section 3, Table 4 and Appendix D directly measure refusal under decoding changes and adversarial suffixes. These results bear on V4 even though the paper's main motivation is compression.

tranche.reason: Compression supplies a new setting for V4. Table 4 reports the study's own refusal-bypass ASRs under decoding and suffix attacks, with uncompressed controls, beyond reporting AIRD performance.

source_check.notes:
The primary PDF's title, authors and arXiv:2504.04215v1 identifier (5 Apr 2025) match the supplied snapshot; no material version differences were found in the checked evidence, and all four required images were inspected successfully with no missing or failed material.
Table 4's unusual column order is genuine, its extraction ambiguity is resolved, and r5 is a stored-cell error; §4 contains a source-internal harmful/harmless validation-set inconsistency, while the compressed-model attack rows also bear on V4 despite their stored none links.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Attack success is higher than the vanilla baseline for both decoding measures and suffixes in the reported Llama3-8b-instruct conditions (r13–r14, r16–r21).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama2 models and Llama3 base/Wanda-Align conditions
reader_labels.reason: Results vary by model and attack measure; several attack rates are below or equal to vanilla, while some rise only partially (r1–r12, r15–r18).
